Which explanation best conveys why Tree-ear responds as he does when watching Min the potter work at the end of Chapter 1?
A. Tree-ear is bored by the slow work and only watches because he has nothing else to do.
Incorrect: The text shows Tree-ear is not bored; he watches “for the hundredth time” and is amazed, which shows strong interest, not boredom.
B. Tree-ear begins to admire Min’s skill and starts to feel interested in learning a craft that requires patience and hard work.
Correct: Tree-ear is fascinated by Min’s patience and perfectionism, which suggests he is beginning to admire skill, hard work, and the idea of learning a craft.
C. Tree-ear feels angry that Min throws away pots that look perfect to him.
Incorrect: Although Tree-ear is confused about why Min rejects pots, he does not feel angry; instead, he wonders what Min sees that he cannot.
D. Tree-ear decides that making pottery would be easy since Min can do it so quickly.
Incorrect: Tree-ear does not think the work is easy; Min’s repeated attempts and high standards show that the craft requires practice and patience.
Briefly explain the concept of central idea or theme in relation to the connections between chapters across a novel.

Authors combine elements such as characters, plot, conflict, setting, and literary devices to communicate meaning through their writing. A chapter’s theme or central idea is the key message or insight revealed through its events and the characters’ reactions. It shows what the chapter is really about beyond the plot. As these ideas develop from chapter to chapter, they build toward the larger themes of the entire text.
Based on what we have read in Chapter 1, what might be one of the themes or central ideas in this chapter? Identify textual evidence that supports your response.

A central idea or theme of Chapter 1 is that Tree-ear learns through his relationship with Crane-man that it is important to be honest, work hard, and have dignity, and he begins to admire the patience and skill of the potter Min. In the text, Crane-man acts as an important guide for Tree-ear. Tree-ear looks to and follows Crane-man’s advice, even when it may be difficult to do so. Tree-ear and Crane-man also work together for their survival. Tree-ear’s interest in Min’s work might suggest that Tree-ear would like to have Min as a mentor.
What details in Chapter 1 show how Tree-ear begins learning by observing the world around him? How do his actions and habits demonstrate the early stages of learning something difficult?
Tree-ear carefully watches people in the village as he scavenges for food. He secretly watches Min as he throws pots on his wheel outside. He begins to learn Min’s processes and routines.
How can observation help spark a person’s interest in something? Describe a time that you became interested in something after observing?
Observation helps you better understand a task; this understanding can help you become more interested as you learn more about how and what to do. Responses will vary.
Struggling with: Using action and interpretive verbs

Explain the difference between action and interpretive verbs when citing evidence. (Ex. Action verbs describe something that someone is doing. For example: observe, notice, and respond. An interpretive verb helps us better understand clues and make inferences in a text. For example, a piece of evidence might reveal, suggest, or indicate.) Citing evidence: Provide evidence-based phrases that students can use when citing evidence in a text. (Ex. On page . . . , this shows . . . The author explains in this paragraph that . . . , This quote . . . suggests . . .)

Why is citing text evidence important when identifying and describing a central idea in a text? Authors may not state a central idea directly in the text. That means readers must look for ways that the author is building meaning. Citing text evidence helps support the inferences, or conclusions, that the reader makes about what the author is saying.
